name: Phoenix Mars Lander
locationName: Vastitas Borealis, the arctic plains of Mars
distanceNote: NASA says Mars is, on average, 140 million miles (about 225 million km) from Earth. The real distance changes all the time as both planets orbit the Sun.
editorNote: Two different 'end' dates appear in NASA sources and both are used on purpose. NSSDCA and the science.nasa.gov quick facts give Nov. 2, 2008 (last signal received), which is lastContact. The JPL release of May 24, 2010 is when NASA said operations had ended after Mars Odyssey heard nothing; the letter calls that 'ended my mission'. Landing time also differs (23:53:44 UT at NSSDCA, 23:38:38 UT at science.nasa.gov); we only state the date, which both agree on.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Phoenix Mars Lander
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 2007-034A; launch August 4, 2007; landing May 25, 2008; Peter H. Smith of the University of Arizona as mission principal investigator; last signal received November 2, 2008.

sources.title: NASA Science: Phoenix
sources.supports: Landing May 25, 2008 on Vastitas Borealis, the arctic plains of Mars; dug into an ice-rich layer near the surface; bright clumps in a trench were water ice that vaporized after about four days; HiRISE photographed Phoenix under its parachute, the first time one spacecraft photographed another during a planetary landing.

sources.title: NASA JPL news, May 24, 2010: Phoenix Mars Lander is Silent, New Image Shows Damage
sources.supports: Mars Odyssey flew over the landing site 61 times in a final attempt to hear from Phoenix; NASA said operations ended in May 2010; ice damage to the solar panels; Peter Smith, principal investigator, at the University of Arizona in Tucson.

sources.title: HiRISE (University of Arizona): Phoenix Lander after One Mars Year
sources.supports: HiRISE image taken May 7, 2010 shows the lander covered in dust with a solar panel that appears to have collapsed; winter carbon dioxide frost weighed the panels down; HiRISE is operated at the University of Arizona.

name: Voyager 1
distanceNote: One light-day, the distance light travels in 24 hours (299,792.458 km per second for 86,400 seconds). NASA rounds it to 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion km). Voyager 1 reaches it on Nov. 18, 2026.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Voyager 1
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 1977-084A; launch September 5, 1977.

sources.title: NASA Science: Where Are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now? (page updated Nov. 12, 2026)
sources.supports: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day, 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion km), on Nov. 18, 2026 at 2:16:07 a.m. PST and is the first human-made object to reach that distance; a light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours; the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem are on and the other instruments are off; it flew past Jupiter and Saturn.

sources.title: NASA Science: Voyager 1 (page updated Nov. 12, 2026)
sources.supports: Launch September 5, 1977; entered interstellar space in August 2012; first human-made object to venture into interstellar space; status 'Extended Mission'; continues to collect data.

name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle (descent stage)
distanceNote: NASA says the Moon is an average of 238,855 miles (384,400 km) from Earth. The real distance changes a little during every orbit.
editorNote: NSSDCA ID 1969-059C covers the whole Lunar Module (both stages) plus the EASEP experiments; this postcard is only about the descent stage, which NSSDCA says was left behind on the Moon. NSSDCA says the fate of the ascent stage is not known, so the letter says nothing about where it ended up. The LROC page describes 'two and a half hours spent on the surface' while NSSDCA's times give a moonwalk of about 2 hours 15 minutes; the content states neither and only uses NSSDCA's 21 hours 36 minutes on the surface.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Apollo 11 Lunar Module / EASEP
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 1969-059C; launch July 16, 1969; landing July 20, 1969 in the Sea of Tranquility; first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon; carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin; four landing legs with round footpads and a ladder; plaque wording 'We came in peace for all mankind' on a strut behind the ladder; 21.55 kg of rock and soil collected; liftoff after 21 hours 36 minutes on the surface; the descent stage served as the launch platform and was left behind; the EASEP included a passive seismometer.

sources.title: LROC (Arizona State University): A Stark Beauty All Its Own
sources.supports: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter image of the Apollo 11 site taken from 24 km (15 miles) above the surface, credited NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University; the Lunar Module and the dark paths of the astronauts' footsteps are visible; the seismic package provided the first lunar seismic data; the samples showed the site was once the site of volcanic activity and lava flows.

sources.title: NASA Science: Apollo 11 Landing Site
sources.supports: The Apollo 11 descent stage, which the astronauts left behind, is visible in the LROC image along with the trails of the astronauts' footprints.

sources.supports: arizonaNote: every astronaut who ever set foot on the Moon trained with the USGS in Flagstaff, Arizona.

name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
distanceNote: NASA says the Moon is an average of 238,855 miles (384,400 km) from Earth. Laser stations measure a distance to the reflectors that swings between about 357,000 and 407,000 km.
editorNote: The reflector's own NSSDCA experiment ID is 1969-059C-04, which the schema's nssdcId pattern does not accept, so nssdcId holds the parent spacecraft ID 1969-059C (Apollo 11 Lunar Module / EASEP). arrivalDate is the landing date (July 20, 1969 UT); the reflector was set out during the moonwalk early on July 21 UT, so the letter only says 'July 1969'. Average Moon distance is given as 384,400 km on NASA's Moon Facts page and rounded to 385,000 km in the 2019 NASA article; the data uses 384,400 km. The 'still working' claim rests on a 2026 conference abstract by NASA Goddard authors (57th LPSC), not on a 2026 NASA web page; a human may want to add a newer NASA page if one appears.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Laser Ranging Retroreflector (Apollo 11)
sources.supports: Experiment ID 1969-059C-04; left on the lunar surface by the Apollo 11 crew; an array of fused silica cubes; laser beams from Earth are reflected back to their point of origin to measure the Earth-Moon distance precisely.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Apollo 11 Lunar Module / EASEP
sources.supports: Launch July 16, 1969; landing July 20, 1969 in the Sea of Tranquility; the laser ranging retroreflector required no power.

sources.title: NASA, July 24, 2019: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving
sources.supports: Buzz Aldrin carried the reflector to its spot; the Apollo 11 array has 100 quartz glass prisms called corner cubes; the arrays need no power; observatories in New Mexico, France, Italy and Germany fire lasers at them and time the round trip; distance measured to within a few millimeters; the Moon moves away from Earth by 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) a year; laser data show the Moon has a fluid core.

sources.title: NASA International Laser Ranging Service: Apollo 11 retroreflector
sources.supports: Deployed in July 1969 by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in Mare Tranquillitatis; more than 50 years later it still yields scientific data; the laser ranging distance is about 357,000 to 407,000 km.

sources.title: Mao et al. (NASA Goddard), 57th Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (2026), abstract 1707: Laser Ranging from LRO-LOLA to Retro-Reflector Arrays on the Lunar Surface
sources.supports: 2026 status: the laser altimeter on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter successfully ranges to the Apollo 11 reflector array from lunar orbit.

sources.title: LROC (Arizona State University): A Stark Beauty All Its Own
sources.supports: arizonaNote: the LROC image, credited NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University, shows the reflector (LRRR) and its discarded cover; the reflector allows precise measurements to this day.

name: Opportunity rover
locationName: Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour Crater, Meridiani Planum
distanceNote: NASA says Mars is, on average, 140 million miles (about 225 million km) from Earth. The real distance changes all the time as both planets orbit the Sun.
editorNote: Dates differ only by time zone. NSSDCA gives launch on July 8, 2003 and landing on January 25, 2004 (both Universal Time); science.nasa.gov gives July 7, 2003 PDT and January 24, 2004 PST for the same moments. The data follows NSSDCA, and the letter only says 'January 2004'. NSSDCA says the rover came to rest in a 20 m crater; science.nasa.gov names it Eagle. Final odometry of 28.06 miles (45.16 km) is from science.nasa.gov; NSSDCA gives no total.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Opportunity
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 2003-032A; launch July 8, 2003 (UT); landing January 25, 2004 (UT) cushioned by airbags, stopping in a small crater; explored for over 14 years; final communication received June 10, 2018; six wheels, solar arrays and an instrument arm.

sources.title: NASA Science: Opportunity
sources.supports: About the size of a golf cart; bounced at least 26 times before stopping in Eagle crater in Meridiani Planum; designed to last 90 Martian days; found a basketball-sized iron-nickel meteorite near its heat shield in January 2005; first to exceed a marathon distance, 26.219 miles (42.195 km), announced March 25, 2015; went quiet in the Mars-wide dust storm of 2018, last signal June 10, 2018; final odometry 28.06 miles (45.16 km); record stood until Perseverance passed it on Oct. 11, 2026; resting spot is Perseverance Valley; NASA declared the mission complete on Feb. 13, 2019.

sources.title: NASA news release 2004-074, March 2, 2004: Opportunity Rover Finds Strong Evidence Meridiani Planum Was Wet
sources.supports: Scientists concluded the part of Mars that Opportunity explored was soaking wet in the past; 'Liquid water once flowed through these rocks'.

sources.title: NASA Science, Oct. 12, 2026: NASA's Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven
sources.supports: On Oct. 11, 2026, a drive pushed Perseverance's total past Opportunity's 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record.

sources.title: HiRISE (University of Arizona): Opportunity Imaged by HiRISE
sources.supports: arizonaNote: HiRISE photographed Opportunity and its wheel tracks from orbit; HiRISE images were routinely used by the Opportunity team to plan drives; HiRISE is operated by the University of Arizona.

sources.supports: distanceKm: Mars is, on average, 140 million miles from Earth.

name: Spirit rover
locationName: Near Home Plate in the Columbia Hills, Gusev Crater
distanceNote: NASA says Mars is, on average, 140 million miles (about 225 million km) from Earth. The real distance changes all the time as both planets orbit the Sun.
editorNote: Landing date differs only by time zone: NSSDCA gives January 4, 2004 (04:35 UT), science.nasa.gov gives January 3, 2004 (20:35 PST). The data follows NSSDCA and the letter only says 'January 2004'. The sources also date the moment Spirit got stuck differently: NSSDCA says it broke through a crust on April 23, 2009 and could not move by May 1; science.nasa.gov says it became stuck on May 1, 2009. The letter only says '2009'.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Spirit
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 2003-027A; launch June 10, 2003; landing January 4, 2004 (UT) in Gusev Crater; six wheels; lost the use of one wheel; stuck in sand in 2009; last transmission March 22, 2010; travelled a total of 7.73 km.

sources.title: NASA Science: Spirit
sources.supports: Opportunity is its twin; first grinding of a rock on Mars with the rock abrasion tool (rock Adirondack); reached the summit of Husband Hill on Sept. 29, 2005 and took 360-degree panoramas; a front wheel stopped working and scraped up bright silica-rich soil, nearly pure silica, likely made by hot springs or steam vents, strong evidence ancient Mars was much wetter; dust devils and wind cleaned the solar panels and raised power; stuck in soft soil beside Home Plate in 2009; no contact after March 22, 2010; NASA ended recovery efforts May 25, 2011; traveled 4.8 miles (7.73 kilometers); operated 6 years, 2 months and 19 days, more than 25 times its intended lifetime.

sources.title: NASA Science: Opportunity
sources.supports: Opportunity landed 20 days after Spirit; both rovers were designed to last 90 Martian days.

sources.title: HiRISE (University of Arizona): Spirit Lander and Bonneville Crater in Color
sources.supports: today and arizonaNote: the rover can still be seen from orbit near Home Plate in the Columbia Hills; its tracks have been erased by the wind; HiRISE is operated by the University of Arizona.

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
locationName: Valinor Hills, its final airfield on Mars
distanceNote: NASA says Mars is, on average, 140 million miles (about 225 million km) from Earth. The real distance changes all the time as both planets orbit the Sun.
editorNote: Ingenuity has no NSSDCA ID of its own; 2020-052A is the Mars 2020 mission (Perseverance) that carried it. lastContact is left out because no page that was opened for this item gives the date of the final signal. 'Valinor Hills' is the team's informal name, taken from the Mastcam-Z team page at Arizona State University. The Arizona note is limited to what the sources show (a Mastcam-Z image credit that includes ASU, and the ASU-hosted Mastcam-Z page); no opened page states who leads Mastcam-Z, so that claim is not made.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Mars 2020 (Perseverance, with the Ingenuity helicopter)
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 2020-052A; launch July 30, 2020; landing February 18, 2021 in Jezero Crater; mass of roughly 1.8 kg; twin counter-rotating blades turning at almost 3000 rpm; mounted on the belly of the rover; flies in the thin Martian atmosphere; first flight April 19, 2021, hovering at 3 meters altitude.

sources.title: NASA Science: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
sources.supports: First powered, controlled flight on another planet on April 19, 2021; designed for no more than five test flights; completed 72 flights across nearly three years; last flight Jan. 18, 2024; mission completed Jan. 25, 2024; 128.8 flying minutes, 10.5 miles (17.0 kilometers), altitudes as high as 78.7 feet (24.0 meters); 3.97 pounds (1.8 kilograms); served as an aerial scout previewing areas for the Perseverance rover.

sources.title: NASA JPL news, Jan. 25, 2024: After Three Years on Mars, NASA's Ingenuity Helicopter Mission Ends
sources.supports: A rotor blade was damaged during the landing of the Jan. 18, 2024 flight and the helicopter can no longer fly; end of mission announced Jan. 25, 2024; a Mastcam-Z picture of Ingenuity is credited NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS.

sources.title: Mastcam-Z (Arizona State University): Sol 1067, Valinor Hills, Ingenuity's Final Resting Place
sources.supports: locationName, today and arizonaNote: the final resting spot is informally named Valinor Hills and is surrounded by sand; Perseverance's Mastcam-Z photographed Ingenuity there; the Mastcam-Z team page is hosted at Arizona State University.

name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle
distanceNote: NASA says the Moon is an average of 238,855 miles (384,400 km) from Earth. The real distance changes a little during every orbit.
editorNote: The rover has no NSSDCA ID of its own; 1972-096C is the Apollo 17 Lunar Module that carried it. Sources disagree slightly on the total distance driven: NSSDCA says 35.9 km, science.nasa.gov says 22.21 miles (35.744 km), and LROC says 'more than 36 kilometers'. The content follows NSSDCA, rounded to 'about 36 km (22 miles)'. The Arizona note uses the USGS statement that every moonwalker trained in Flagstaff; the USGS page does not name the Apollo 17 crew or say they trained at Cinder Lake, so neither is claimed.

sources.title: NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle
sources.supports: An electric vehicle; driven on Apollo 17 by Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt on three traverses; went 35.9 km; greatest range from the lunar module 7.6 km; folded and stored in the lunar module; two side-by-side seats; tires of woven steel strands; each wheel had its own electric drive motor; TV camera; Harrison Schmitt's statement that the major discoveries of Apollo 15, 16 and 17 would not have been possible without the rover.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Apollo 17 Lunar Module / ALSEP
sources.supports: NSSDCA ID 1972-096C; launch December 7, 1972; landing December 11, 1972 in the Taurus-Littrow area; the lunar module carried the Lunar Roving Vehicle; 110.52 kg of lunar samples collected; Schmitt discovered a patch of orange soil on the second moonwalk.

sources.title: LROC (Arizona State University): Apollo 17 Remains Unchallenged After Fifty Years
sources.supports: Cernan parked the rover so its video camera could capture the liftoff; the farthest drive reached about 4.7 miles (7.6 kilometers) from the lunar module; the landing site hardware remains preserved on the surface; LROC continues to image the Apollo sites.

sources.title: NASA Science: Opportunity
sources.supports: today: on May 16, 2013 NASA announced Opportunity had passed the record for the farthest distance traveled by any NASA vehicle on another celestial body, set by the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle in December 1972 (22.21 miles).
